title: Hydraulics: pressure, flow, pumps, F = pA
goals: Work out a hydraulic cylinder's force from its bore and the pressure
Work out a cylinder's speed from the flow, extending and retracting
Work out a pump's flow from its displacement and speed, and the power it needs
Say what the relief valve does, and why the load, not the pump, sets the pressure
Make a hydraulic system safe: pressure, accumulators and suspended loads
summary:
Hydraulics pushes oil, which hardly compresses, at high pressure: 100–250 bar is common, against about 6 bar for air. So small cylinders give big forces and hold position firmly.

**Force**: $F = pA$. With p in bar: $F = 0.1 \times p \times A$ newtons, A in mm². Push on the full bore; pull on the annulus (bore less rod).

**Speed**: the oil fills the cylinder: $v = \frac{Q}{A}$. With Q in L/min, divide by 60 000 for m³/s and use A in m². Retracting is **faster** than extending, because the annulus is smaller.

**Pump**: a positive-displacement pump (gear, vane, piston) delivers a fixed volume per turn: $Q = \frac{V n}{1000}$ L/min, with V in cm³/rev and n in rpm (a little less in practice: volumetric efficiency).

The **pump makes flow; the load makes pressure**. Pressure rises until the oil can move the load, or until the **relief valve** opens at its setting, which caps the system's pressure (and so its force).

**Power**: $P = \frac{p Q}{600}$ kW, with p in bar and Q in L/min. The motor must give that divided by the pump's overall efficiency.

A typical circuit: **tank**, suction **strainer**, **pump**, **relief valve**, **filter**, **directional valve** (often a 4/3), **cylinder** or **motor**, back to tank.

**Safety**: oil at 200 bar through a pinhole can inject into skin: never feel for leaks. **Accumulators** store pressure after the pump stops: discharge them. Block or lower suspended loads before opening anything.

formulas.name: Cylinder force
formulas.says: The oil's pressure times the area it pushes on.
formulas.example: 63 mm bore at 160 bar: $16 \times 3117 = 49\,900$ N, about 50 kN.

formulas.name: Cylinder speed
formulas.says: The oil has to fill the cylinder; the more flow, or the smaller the area, the faster the piston goes.

formulas.name: Pump flow
formulas.says: Each turn delivers the pump's displacement; times turns a minute gives cm³ a minute; ÷ 1000 for litres.
formulas.example: 16 cm³/rev at 1450 rpm: $\frac{16 \times 1450}{1000} = 23.2$ L/min (a little less in practice).

formulas.name: Hydraulic power
formulas.says: Power is pressure times flow; with bar and L/min, dividing by 600 gives kW.

bench.task: On a hydraulic power pack you are authorised to work on, read its data and check the sums. Machine isolated, pressure released and any accumulator discharged before touching any fitting.
check: Read the pump's displacement (cm³/rev) and the motor's speed and power from their plates
Work out the flow and, at the relief setting on the drawing, the power the pump needs
Check that is within the motor's rating
Find the relief valve and the gauge, and any accumulator and its discharge valve

cards.q: A hydraulic pump is running and a cylinder is extending freely with no load. The relief valve is set to 180 bar. Roughly what does the pressure gauge read?
options: Low: just enough to move the piston and oil
180 bar, the relief setting
Whatever the pump's rating is
Zero, until the cylinder stops
cards.why: The pump makes flow; the load makes pressure. With nothing resisting, the pressure only rises as far as friction and the pipes need. It climbs to 180 bar when the cylinder meets a load it cannot move, or hits the end of its stroke, and the relief valve opens.

cards.title: Big forces from small cylinders
cards.body:
Pressure acts on every square millimetre of the piston, so as with air:

$$F = pA$$

With $p$ in bar, use $0.1 \times p$ N/mm². Hydraulics runs at **100–250 bar** or more, about 30 times shop air, so a 63 mm cylinder at 160 bar pushes about **50 kN**: five tonnes.

Oil hardly compresses, so a hydraulic cylinder **holds** its position firmly (as long as nothing leaks).
cards.more:
Same rule as pneumatics; the numbers are just much bigger.

63 mm bore: area $\pi \times 63^2 \div 4 = 3117$ mm². At 160 bar (16 N/mm²): $16 \times 3117 = 49\,872$ N, about 50 kN.

The same cylinder on 6 bar of air would push under 2 kN.

Retracting, the oil pushes on the annulus, as with air: a 63 mm bore with a 36 mm rod has $\pi (63^2 - 36^2) \div 4 = 2099$ mm², so 33.6 kN pull at 160 bar.

cards.q: A hydraulic cylinder has a {bore} mm bore and works at {bar} bar. What force does it push with, in kN?
cards.why: Bar × 0.1 is N/mm²; × the area in mm² gives N; ÷ 1000 for kN.

cards.title: Speed comes from flow
cards.body:
The piston moves as fast as the oil can fill the space behind it:

$$v = \frac{Q}{A}$$

$v$ in m/s, $Q$ the flow in m³/s, $A$ the area being filled in m². Pumps are rated in **L/min**: divide by **60 000** for m³/s.

Retracting, the oil fills only the annulus, which is smaller, so with the same flow the piston comes back **faster** than it went out.
cards.more:
Think of filling a bucket from a hose: a narrow bucket fills to the top sooner than a wide one. The piston is the water level.

Numbers: 20 L/min is $20 \div 60\,000 = 0.000333$ m³/s. A 63 mm bore is $\pi \times 0.063^2 \div 4 = 0.003117$ m². So $0.000333 \div 0.003117 = 0.107$ m/s, about 107 mm a second.

With a 36 mm rod, the annulus is 0.002099 m²: retracting at 0.159 m/s.

More pressure does not make it faster; more flow does. Pressure is for force; flow is for speed.

cards.q: {q} L/min flows into the full-bore side of a cylinder with a {bore} mm bore. How fast does it extend?
cards.why: Flow in m³/s over the area in m². L/min ÷ 60 000 is m³/s; mm ÷ 1000 is m.
cards.hint: Get both into SI: L/min ÷ 60 000, and the bore in metres.

cards.title: The pump makes flow; the load makes pressure
cards.body:
Hydraulic pumps (gear, vane, piston) are **positive displacement**: each turn pushes out a fixed volume, the **displacement** $V$ in cm³/rev:

$$Q = \frac{V n}{1000}$$

$Q$ in L/min, $n$ in rpm. Real pumps leak a little inside: a **volumetric efficiency** of about 0.9–0.95.

The pump does not make pressure. The **load** does: pressure rises until the oil can move whatever resists it. The **relief valve** caps it: at its setting it opens and sends the flow back to tank.
cards.more:
A positive-displacement pump is like a syringe pushed at a steady rate: the plunger moves whatever is in the way, or something gives.

That is why the relief valve is vital: with the cylinder at the end of its stroke and nowhere for the oil to go, the pressure would rise until a hose burst or the pump broke. The relief valve is the 'something gives', set just above the working pressure.

While the relief valve is blowing, all the pump's power turns into heat in the oil: a power pack left pushing against a stop gets hot fast. Unloading circuits or pressure-compensated pumps avoid that.

Numbers: 16 cm³/rev at 1450 rpm gives $16 \times 1450 \div 1000 = 23.2$ L/min, about 22 L/min in practice.

cards.q: A pump with a displacement of {disp} cm³/rev turns at {rpm} rpm. What flow does it give, in theory?
cards.why: Displacement × speed is cm³ a minute; 1000 cm³ is a litre.
cards.hint: cm³ per turn × turns a minute, then ÷ 1000 for litres.

cards.q: What sets the highest pressure a hydraulic system can reach?
options: The relief valve's setting
The pump's displacement
The size of the tank
The cylinder's bore
cards.why: A positive-displacement pump will push its flow against anything; the relief valve opens at its setting and caps the pressure. The bore sets the force at that pressure.

cards.title: Hydraulic power
cards.body:
Power is pressure times flow. With **bar** and **L/min**:

$$P = \frac{p Q}{600}$$

$P$ in **kW**. The motor driving the pump must give this divided by the pump's **overall efficiency** (about 0.85 for a good gear pump, more for a piston pump).

Power that does no useful work (through the relief valve, across a throttle) becomes **heat** in the oil.
cards.more:
Where does the 600 come from? Power in watts is pressure in Pa times flow in m³/s. 1 bar is 100 000 Pa; 1 L/min is $\frac{1}{60\,000}$ m³/s. So bar × L/min × $\frac{100\,000}{60\,000}$ gives watts, and ÷ 1000 for kW: altogether ÷ 600.

Numbers: 160 bar at 30 L/min: $160 \times 30 \div 600 = 8$ kW of hydraulic power. At 85% overall efficiency the motor must give $8 \div 0.85 = 9.4$ kW: an 11 kW motor.

If the relief valve is blowing at 160 bar all the time, those 8 kW are heating the oil: that is a cooler's job, or a better circuit.

cards.q: A pump delivers {q} L/min at {bar} bar. What hydraulic power is that?
cards.why: Pressure times flow; with bar and L/min, ÷ 600 gives kW.

cards.title: Making hydraulics safe
cards.body:
- **Isolate** the power pack, then **release the pressure**: stopping the pump is not enough.
- **Accumulators** store oil under gas pressure and keep it after the pump stops: **discharge** them through their dump valve and check the gauge reads zero.
- **Suspended loads** (a raised platen, a boom) are held up by trapped oil: **lower or block** them mechanically before opening anything.
- A pinhole leak at 100+ bar can **inject oil through skin**: never feel for leaks with your hands; use card. An injection is a hospital emergency even if it looks small.
- Oil is slippery and can be hot.
cards.more:
The danger is energy that stays after the machine is 'off'. A pump stopping only stops new oil. Oil trapped behind a check valve holding up a press tool, or in an accumulator, is still at full pressure.

Loosening a fitting on such a line releases it at once: the load drops, or a jet of oil comes out.

Injection injuries are easy to underestimate: a small mark on the hand, but oil under the skin spreads and kills tissue. Hospitals treat it as urgent surgery.

The lock-off procedure for a hydraulic machine lists these steps in order: isolate, lower or block loads, discharge accumulators, prove zero pressure on the gauges.

cards.q: Put the steps of making a hydraulic press safe in order.
items: Lower the platen or block it mechanically
Stop and isolate the power pack, and lock it off
Discharge the accumulator through its dump valve
cards.why: Deal with the load while you still have control of it, then remove the energy source, then the stored energy, then prove it.

cards.q: A cylinder with an 80 mm bore and a 45 mm rod is fed 25 L/min at up to 150 bar. Find its push force, its extend speed and its retract speed.

steps.ask: The annulus area, and the retract speed.

cards.why: Pressure and area give force; flow and area give speed. The rod side is smaller, so it comes back faster with less force.

cards.q: Why does the cylinder retract faster than it extends, with the same pump?
cards.context: Extend 0.083 m/s on 5027 mm²; retract 0.121 m/s on 3436 mm².
cards.model: The pump delivers the same flow either way. Retracting, the oil only has to fill the ring around the rod, which is a smaller volume per millimetre of stroke than the full bore. The same litres a minute fill a smaller space faster, so the piston moves faster. The price is force: less area means less force at the same pressure.
points: The annulus is smaller than the bore
Faster but weaker on the rod side

cards.q: A power pack must give 30 L/min at 140 bar. The pump's overall efficiency is 0.85. What motor power?

steps.show: The next standard size up: 11 kW (7.5 kW would be too small).

cards.why: Work the useful power, divide by the efficiency, then round up to a standard motor size, never down.

cards.q: A pump must give {q} L/min at {bar} bar, with an overall efficiency of {eff}. What power must the motor give, in kW?
cards.why: Hydraulic power, divided by the efficiency (the motor also supplies what the pump loses).

cards.q: {q} L/min feeds the rod side of a cylinder: bore {bore} mm, rod {rod} mm. How fast does it retract?
cards.why: On the rod side, the oil fills the annulus: the bore's area less the rod's.
cards.hint: Annulus area in m², flow in m³/s.

cards.q: A press needs {kn} kN at {bar} bar. What is the smallest bore that will do it?
cards.why: Area = force ÷ pressure; then the diameter for that area. Choose the next standard bore up.
cards.hint: kN × 1000 for N; bar × 0.1 for N/mm².

cards.q: The power pack is switched off and locked. Why can a hydraulic line still be at full pressure?
options: An accumulator or a trapped load holds it
Hydraulic oil expands as it cools down
The pump keeps turning on its own
Gauges lag behind by several minutes
cards.why: An accumulator stores oil under gas pressure, and a load held up by a check valve keeps its oil pressurised. Both stay after the pump stops: discharge and lower before opening anything.

cards.q: Working out a 50 mm bore cylinder's speed on 12 L/min. One line is wrong. Which?
cards.fix: Area: $\pi \times 0.05^2 \div 4 = 0.001963$ m², so the speed is $0.0002 \div 0.001963 = 0.10$ m/s
cards.why: The bore was used in mm while the flow was in m³/s, so the area came out a million times too big. Units check: m³/s divided by m² gives m/s only if the area really is in m².

cards.q: A power pack's oil gets very hot when a cylinder is held against its end stop for long periods. Why?
options: All the pump's flow crosses the relief valve as heat
Hydraulic oil heats up whenever it is still
The cylinder seals rub on the stop
The tank is too full of oil
cards.why: With the cylinder stopped, the pump's flow goes over the relief valve at full pressure: all that power becomes heat. A pressure-compensated pump or an unloading valve avoids it.

cards.q: The same {bore} mm bore cylinder on 6 bar air, then on {bar} bar hydraulics. How many times more force does the hydraulic one give?
cards.work: Same area, so the ratio is the pressures: ${bar} \div 6 = {answer}$
cards.why: F = pA with the same A: the force goes with the pressure. The bore cancels out.
cards.hint: What stays the same, and what changes?

cards.q: A cylinder is too slow but strong enough. What do you change?
options: More flow (a bigger pump, or less throttling)
More pressure (raise the relief valve)
A bigger bore cylinder
A longer stroke
cards.why: Speed comes from flow; force from pressure. Raising the pressure would not speed it up, and a bigger bore would slow it down on the same flow.

cards.q: A {disp} cm³/rev pump runs at {rpm} rpm against a relief setting of {bar} bar. What hydraulic power does it put out at full pressure, in kW (theory)?
cards.why: Two rules in a row: displacement × speed for the flow, then pressure × flow for the power.

cards.q: A hydraulic cylinder is extending with no load. The pressure on the gauge is low. Why is it not at the relief setting?
options: Pressure only rises to what the load needs
The pump is undersized for the job
The relief valve is faulty
The gauge is reading flow, not pressure
cards.why: The pump makes flow; the load makes pressure. With nothing to push, little pressure is needed.

cards.q: {bore} mm bore at {bar} bar. Push force in kN?
cards.why: F = pA, bar × 0.1 for N/mm², ÷ 1000 for kN.

cards.q: {q} L/min at {bar} bar. Hydraulic power?
cards.why: Pressure × flow, ÷ 600 for kW with bar and L/min.
